elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New Section 11.4: "Corio (as customer) may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". Corio is the customer/licensee party, so the right runs in the correct direction; the element is disjunctive and this Agreement has no Order Form structure, so Agreement-level termination suffices.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: 11.4 sets "thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly 30 days, written, and no additional conditions or approvals attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: 11.4: "Commerce One shall refund pro rata any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination." The refund is expressly pro rata (not merely post-termination-period) and the payer is the Vendor.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: 11.4: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Section 11.2 gives Commerce One only breach/insolvency exits, and the 11.1 notice is natural-term non-renewal (expressly tied to expiration of the then-current term), evaluated under RENEWAL, so no retained sentence contradicts the bar.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: 11.4 gives 30 days' notice, which is outside the literal 60–90 day fallback band (though more favourable to Customer). The preferred level is achieved instead.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither Section 11 as retained nor new 11.4 imposes any early-termination fee, penalty, instalment acceleration, or contingent payment on Corio's convenience exit, so there is nothing above a three-month cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Satisfied a fortiori: 11.4 bars Commerce One from any convenience termination during the initial or renewal terms, and 11.1's only term-end notice right is expressly tied to expiration of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No Vendor convenience right survives 11.4, but the retained 11.1 non-renewal mechanic (a RENEWAL matter, not mid-term T4C) runs on 30 days. As a pure convenience-notice element the condition does not apply; it is marked not_met only because the fallback level is not the target and its first element already fails — no repair is required if the preferred level is accepted.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements appear in operative language in new Section 11.4 (customer-side convenience right, 30 days' written notice, express pro rata refund of prepaid fees by Vendor, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the initial five-year term and any renewal term).

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a naming artifact, not a substantive gap: the drafter used lowercase "(as customer)" to avoid colliding with the Section 1.6 defined term CUSTOMER(S), and named Corio expressly, so the operative grant is unambiguous and leaves no undefined term or dangling reference.

Minimality holds: Sections 11.1–11.3 are untouched, no Customer-favourable language is deleted, and the insertion adds no survival tail, expense allocation, procedure, or extra remedy. The model-language phrase "in whole or in part" was correctly dropped because there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure in this Agreement.

Intent is preserved: the 11.3 survival architecture (including Corio's post-termination Customer access rights and Commerce One's continuing support obligation against continued payment) and the 11.1 renewal mechanic operate without contradiction; the 11.4 bar on Vendor convenience termination does not disturb the 11.2 breach/insolvency exits, which remain mutual.

The "deviation" finding is correct on the original text — the five-year committed term with no Customer convenience exit fails even the fallback — and the non-renewal notice in 11.1 was properly left to RENEWAL rather than double-flagged here.
